chapter: Banjo, piano and his own bands
title: Learning piano, Bill Russell, the Banner Club and Burnell
summary: Bill Russell asked about Jelly Roll Morton, whom he cooked Monday dinners for; he learned piano on a club piano, played the Banner Club with George, and praises pianist Burnell.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught

blocks.x: You just play the same note? Yeah. I got a friend of mine who plays the live part of one right now. A five string banjo. He's a guitar player too. He's from here? Yeah, he's a boy from here. He'll play at the... He'll play at the... at the Preservation Hall. He's a good guitar player. He's a guitar player like Sam. A good guitar player and a good banjo player. What's his name? I just forgot him. I ain't seen him in so long. Yeah. I forgot him. And he has a five string banjo? He's got a five string banjo. I met him at the hospital when I was getting my eyes treated. Not Sunday. He's a bright looking boy. God, he's dead. I got a five string banjo player. I'm playing my body. I'm still playing my guitar too, you know? I say, yeah, okay. And who else? I even give Bill Russell a demonstration about General Roll movement. Because I went there to buy some strings, you know? And he said, by the way, he said, you know General Roll? I said, do I know him? I said, I hope I do know him. I said, I used to be with him every Monday. Every Monday. Every Monday, we cook a bean dinner for him. And, you know, serve him the dinner. And he'd be playing the piano. I said, I thought, man, I should have liked to know how to play piano. I wasn't playing. And then, you know? So, they bought the club, bought a piano. I was trying to put it upstairs and threw a rope. Put it up there. And I began to practice. I said, man, why don't you get off that piano? I said, man, I'm paying my dues here. I said, I'm supposed to play this piano all day long if I want. So, I began to practice on the piano, practice and practice until I learned how to play. I was playing. I was playing. We played at the—George and I played at the Banner Club for a long time. The man went to give us 90 hours a week and collect the tips. George said, no, indeed. We were ready to tips. Give us our little change which you give us a week and we'll collect the tips. Boy, I was making something at the Banner Club on Dolph Head Street in the 500 block right next door to where Burnell was playing. You know Burnell, huh? Yeah. Piano player boy now? Heard of him. You heard of him. You never heard of him play? No. Boy, he was a piano player. He was a piano player. I classed him as the best piano player in the state of Louisiana. Fingers like lightning. Good, good. God, the man never really knew. Fingers just like lightning. He was playing right next door to us. I don't know that man's name. Well, you know Sam Hopkins? Uh-huh. Well, that's my piano player now. Sam. But we don't—you know, people didn't kind of read all the piano. I don't know. Yeah. And whenever I get a job playing piano, we got a job we've been playing over the river for the last past seven years with some school teachers, you know? Every year. I got to call that lady up to find out if she wanted to see a condition. But Sam, he can't play. He's working. He works at the IA News. He can't play. In the daytime. There's just a day—a morning job.
